summary.text: The Constitution of the United States is the supreme law of the country, and it replaced the Articles of Confederation on March 4, 1789.
It was drafted at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787, and its first three articles divide the federal government into legislative, executive and judicial branches.
It has been amended 27 times, and the first ten amendments, called the Bill of Rights, protect individual liberty and justice.

facts.label: Standing
facts.value: Oldest written national constitution still in force

items.prompt: When a military crisis hit under the Articles of Confederation, why could Congress not pay for a response?

options.label: It was forbidden to print notes or borrow from other countries
It had no credit or taxing power, and states paid little or nothing
It had been ordered to pay its debts before it could spend
It relied on one wealthy state to fund every government need

items.explain: Congress had no credit or taxing power to finance a response, and no state paid its full share.

items.prompt: A state ignores a decision made under the Articles of Confederation. Why could the Confederation Congress do little about it?

options.label: The Supreme Court had to approve every decision first
The president alone was allowed to act against a state
The Congress lacked powers to enforce its decisions
The decisions applied only to states that had voted for them

items.explain: The Confederation Congress had some decision-making abilities but lacked enforcement powers.

items.prompt: Congress makes the laws, the president carries them out, and the Supreme Court judges disputes. What doctrine does this split of work show?

options.label: The separation of powers
Federalism
Ratification
Amendment

items.explain: The first three articles divide the federal government into legislative, executive and judicial branches, which embodies the separation of powers.

items.prompt: How do amendments to the US Constitution differ from those in many constitutions worldwide?

options.label: They are written into the original articles
They are appended to the document
They are voted on by each state separately
They replace the earlier text of the article

items.explain: Amendments to the US Constitution, unlike those in many constitutions, are appended to the document.

items.prompt: During an uprising in Massachusetts in 1786–1787, Congress could not fund help for the state. How was an army raised?

options.label: Congress borrowed from the Viceroy of Canada
Each state sent its share of troops and pay
The king of Spain lent money to the state
General Benjamin Lincoln raised funds from Boston merchants

items.explain: Congress could provide no money, so General Lincoln raised funds from Boston merchants to pay for a volunteer army.

items.prompt: Britain and the United States signed a peace treaty naming each state, yet several states violated it. What does this show about the Articles?

options.label: It worked well, since the states joined forces to follow the treaty
It was too strict, since it banned states from defending themselves
It failed to bring unity, as states acted on their own against its letter and spirit
It was ignored by Britain, since the treaty covered only Congress

items.explain: States prosecuted Loyalists, negotiated with foreign authorities and raised armies, showing the Articles were failing to unify the states.

paragraphs.heading: The supreme law
paragraphs.text: The Constitution of the United States is the highest law of the country. It began with seven articles that laid out the basic structure of the federal government. It replaced the nation's first constitution, the Articles of Confederation, on March 4, 1789. Today it is the oldest written and codified national constitution still in force anywhere in the world.

paragraphs.heading: The first attempt
paragraphs.text: The Articles of Confederation were drafted by a committee of the Second Continental Congress in 1777 and adopted by Congress that November. Getting all 13 states to ratify them took more than three years, until March 1, 1781. The Articles gave the central government very little power. Congress could make some decisions but had no way to enforce them, and most choices, even changes to the Articles, needed the approval of every state legislature.

paragraphs.heading: No money, no defense
paragraphs.text: George Washington summed up the main problem as "no money". Congress could print money, but it was worthless, and it could borrow but not repay. No state paid its share of taxes and some paid nothing, and by 1786 the country faced default on its debts. The army had just 625 men, its soldiers went unpaid, and when Barbary pirates seized American merchant ships, the Treasury had nothing to pay ransom with.

paragraphs.heading: States going their own way
paragraphs.text: The Articles were also failing to unite states with very different interests. Some states broke the 1783 Treaty of Paris with Britain, and New York and South Carolina kept prosecuting Loyalists and taking their land. State legislatures set their own embargoes, dealt directly with foreign powers, raised armies and even made war. During Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts, Congress could give the threatened state no money, so General Benjamin Lincoln had to raise funds from Boston merchants for a volunteer army.

paragraphs.heading: Framing a new plan
paragraphs.text: Many of the Founding Fathers drafted a new constitution at the Constitutional Convention, which met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787. This drafting is often called the framing. The framers drew on English common law and on Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke and Montesquieu.

paragraphs.heading: How the articles divide power
paragraphs.text: The first three articles follow the idea of separation of powers, which splits government into three branches. The legislature is Congress, which has two chambers; the president leads the executive; and the Supreme Court sits at the top of the judiciary. Articles IV, V and VI deal with federalism: they describe the rights and duties of state governments and how the states relate to the federal government, and they set out how the Constitution can be amended. Article VII describes how the Constitution was to be ratified.

paragraphs.heading: Amendments
paragraphs.text: Since 1789 the Constitution has been amended 27 times. Unlike changes to many constitutions elsewhere, these amendments are attached to the end of the document. The first ten, together called the Bill of Rights, protect individual liberty and justice and limit what government can do. Amendments 13 to 15 are called the Reconstruction Amendments, and most later ones widen civil rights protections.
